The DPA fined a company operating sports centres €96,000 for implementing mandatory facial recognition systems to enter and exit the premises, without the prior knowledge or consent of its members.

Decision 27/2025 of the Greek data protection authority. A woman complained that at least 15 prepaid mobile numbers had been registered in her name, using her ID data, without her knowledge. The activations were made by DS Phone, a Vodafone franchisee acting as its processor, and she was later summoned by prosecutors as a suspect in fraud investigations. Under the GDPR the authority fined Vodafone-Panafon EUR 350,000 for failing in its duties towards its processor (Art. 28) and EUR 200,000 for keeping inaccurate data (Art. 5(1)(d)): EUR 550,000 in all, the figure shown. It added a EUR 150,000 fine under the national e-privacy law (Law 3471/2006) for inadequate security measures, fined the processor DS Phone EUR 40,000, and warned Vodafone to introduce stronger technical measures such as an SMS alert to the subscriber.

A Vodafone subscriber complained that unknown persons had registered at least 15 prepaid mobile numbers in her name using her ID data. It emerged that the franchise shop, acting as Vodafone's processor, had activated 14 prepaid lines for a tourist group by attaching the complainant's ID file from an earlier visit to another shop, by mistake. The Authority found the shop infringed Articles 32 and 29 GDPR and fined it EUR 40,000. It also fined Vodafone separately (EUR 350,000, EUR 200,000 and EUR 150,000) and issued a warning to it; those parts concern Vodafone, not the shop.

The DPA reprimanded the Danish Agency for Digitalization for the insecure processing of personal data via its digital post system, in violation of Article 32 GDPR. The system suffered five data breaches that affected hundreds of thousands of data subjects.

A hospital doctor complained that the head of his clinic collected and used statistics on his operating times, overtime and material use, named per doctor, to exclude him from a hospital laboratory, without informing him, and that his access request went unanswered. The Authority rejected the complaint as inadmissible against the clinic head personally, and held the hospital liable as controller. It fined the hospital EUR 7,000 in total: EUR 4,000 for breaching Article 5, EUR 1,500 for Article 14 and EUR 1,500 for Article 15. It also reprimanded the hospital for breaching Article 31 (late cooperation with the Authority).

The DPA fined an association for people with autism €10,000 for failing to comply with an access request by the legal guardians of a child and for unlawfully transmitting the child’s personal data to third parties.

The UK Information Commissioner issued a penalty notice of £18,000 to Birthlink, an Edinburgh charity running the Adoption Contact Register. Personal data in Linked Records, some highly sensitive, was destroyed without authorisation in April 2021 because of inadequate security measures and limited data protection knowledge among staff. Birthlink only notified the Commissioner of the breach in September 2023, about two years and five months late. The Commissioner found infringements of the UK GDPR principles and security and breach-notification rules and treated them as one penalty.

The Irish DPC announced its final decision on an inquiry into a personal data breach at CDETB, where a webserver retained grant applicants' personal data and malware was found on it. The DPC found infringements of the security principle and security measures (Arts 5(1)(f), 32(1), 32(2)), late notification to the DPC (Art 33(1)), and failures to notify data subjects (Art 34(1) and 34(4)). It reprimanded CDETB, imposed fines totalling EUR 125,000 and ordered it to bring its processing into compliance. The fine was well below the draft range of up to EUR 210,000 because CDETB accepted the findings, took responsibility, apologised and took steps to prevent recurrence.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation into Vodafone Romania in May 2025, started after the company notified a personal data breach under Article 33 GDPR. It found that Vodafone had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures for data protection by design and by default, which led to unauthorised disclosure of and access to customers' data. Vodafone was fined RON 20,226 (about EUR 4,000) and ordered to implement a mechanism for regularly testing and assessing the effectiveness of its security measures.

A complainant received information letters from Piraeus Bank treating him as a guarantor of a relative's business loan, although he had no such role; a bank employee had entered him wrongly in the system. The bank sent a third letter even after he objected. The authority found no proof that his data were passed to the special purpose entity or to the servicer Intrum, and found no breach of the right to object (Art. 21) and no breach by Intrum. It found the bank processed inaccurate data without a legal basis, breaching Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(d) and 6(1), and fined it EUR 50,000.

A report to the Garante revealed that a website linked to the Order of Nursing Professions of Viterbo exposed, without any authentication, a control panel giving access to and editing of the personal data of about 2,500 registered nurses. The exposure lasted from July 2020 to April 2024 and was caused by a web provider's error during a site migration. The Garante found violations of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) GDPR. It fined the Order EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the page had been removed.

A trade union complained on behalf of employees of a transport company that shift tables, posted on company notice boards and emailed to staff, showed reasons for absence (sickness, injury, disability leave, union leave, hospital stay, blood donation) through short codes. The Garante found this disclosed special-category data to staff who had no need to know it, with no lawful basis under Article 9(2) and in breach of data minimisation. The company had already replaced the codes with a generic 'A', so no further corrective measures were needed. The Garante fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A former municipal councillor complained that his personal data, including a declaration of no incompatibility, remained published on the municipality's transparency web page after he resigned. The Garante found that Article 20 of Legislative Decree 39/2013 did not apply to councillors, so there was no legal basis for publication, and that the published data (birth date and place, residence, domicile, handwritten signature) was excessive. It also found that the municipality had only belatedly notified the change of its DPO contact details. Because the violation was minor and the municipality was small and cooperative, the Garante issued a reprimand instead of a fine.

Neighbours complained that a camera mounted by their neighbour on his buildings filmed their courtyard, house and people, and that a drone was also used. The Inspectorate found that Camera No. 1 recorded part of the complainants' driveway and outbuildings, land the neighbour did not own. The household exemption did not apply to that part, and the processing breached the principles of lawfulness and data minimisation. The neighbour was ordered to stop filming the complainants' land by 2025-07-18. The erasure-right complaint was rejected for lack of evidence of a request, and the drone complaint was closed as falling under the household exemption.

A parent complained that footage of their minor daughter, recorded at a school, had left the school's custody and ended up with the Guardia Civil, and that the recordings were made without consent or information. The Spanish AEPD opened a sanctioning procedure against the school for breaches of Article 5(1)(f), Article 6(1) and Article 13 GDPR, with a proposed fine of EUR 40,000. The school acknowledged responsibility and paid, taking two 20% reductions, so the reduced fine is EUR 24,000. The decision terminates the procedure and orders the school to show security measures, stop the unlawful recording and provide the required information within three months.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in May 2025 into SC Diamir SRL after a complaint that it displayed a person's identity card at its place of work, revealing name, address, ID number and photo. The company did not provide the information the authority requested during the investigation, and it disclosed the person's data without consent or any other legal basis. It received a warning for the failure to cooperate and a fine of 5,084.80 lei (about EUR 1,000) for the unlawful disclosure.

A ferry captain employed by a contractor of Stockholm public transport company SL complained about mandatory breathalyser tests before each departure, whose results were logged. IMY found that SL processed the complainant's data between October 2021 and August 2022 without a legal basis under Article 6 and, as health data, without any Article 9(2) exemption. It treated the violations as low severity but not minor enough for a reprimand, found SL negligent, and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 75,000.

IMY investigated a complaint from a ship's master employed by a contractor of the Stockholm public transport authority, about daily breathalyser tests with logged results. IMY found that the company Waxholms Ångfartygs AB processed the complainant's data without a legal basis under Article 6 and processed sensitive health data without any Article 9(2) exception applying, in 2020 and 2021-2022. The violations were assessed as low severity, since the aim was transport safety and the complainant was not directly identifiable. IMY rejected a reprimand and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 75,000. The maximum was calculated on the turnover of the whole SL group, treated as one undertaking.

The DPA issued a warning against the deployment of a “Smart Policing” system by the Hellenic Police, involving smart portable devices used by patrols to determent and verify the identity of citizens subject to on-the-spot checks via the use of biometric data. The DPA considers this processing of personal data unlawful.

The Lithuanian supervisory authority carried out a planned inspection of UAB Diagnostikos laboratorija on how it handles data subject access requests. It found that the controller had not set retention periods for documents relating to access requests, and kept some of them for only one year although it must be able to prove lawful processing for two years, which breached Article 24(1) GDPR. It also found that the controller did not tell requesters when their request would be handled, which breached Article 12(3) GDPR. The authority ordered the controller to set the retention periods and to inform requesters of the handling time, by 11 August 2025. No fine was imposed, and the other parts of the inspection (Article 12 format, content and restrictions) found no non-compliance.
The DPA fined a utilities company €3,000 for processing data without a legal basis, violating Article 6(1) GDPR.
The DPA fined a processor €12,000 for subcontracting another processor without the authorisation of the controller in violation of Article 28(2) GDPR.

The DPA fined a cinema chain €18,000 for automatically including another person's personal data during a customer’s purchase of movie tickets using the controller’s app, in violation of the principles of data accuracy and security of processing.

The Irish DPC announced its final decision in an inquiry into the Department of Social Protection's use of biometric facial templates and facial matching in SAFE 2 registration for the Public Services Card. It found that the Department had not identified a valid lawful basis for collecting the biometric data at the time of the inquiry, and that, following from that, keeping the data also infringed the GDPR; that the information given to people was not transparent enough; and that its data protection impact assessment (DPIA) left out certain required details. The DPC reprimanded the Department, fined it a total of EUR 550,000, and ordered it to stop processing biometric data for SAFE 2 registration within 9 months of the decision if it cannot identify a valid lawful basis.

The DPA held that information about visits to a website’s subpages, containing content on particular medical issues, constitute sensitive data. Therefore, the DPA reprimanded a company for unlawfully processing this sensitive information via the Meta pixel.

The Norwegian DPA carried out a digital inspection of six websites' use of tracking tools. On the children's helpline website 116111.no, run by Kristiansand municipality, it found Meta Pixel and Snap Pixel sending visitors' data to Meta and Snap without a valid legal basis, and the privacy notice did not mention the pixels or the sharing. The DPA fined the municipality NOK 250,000 for breaching Article 6(1) and the information duties in Articles 12(1) and 13. In setting the amount it weighed the importance of the service for vulnerable children, the municipality's strained finances and its clean-up measures. The municipality had removed the pixels after the notice of decision.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in May 2025 into Accounting Audit SRL, acting as a processor for its clients. A cyberattack led to unauthorised disclosure of personal data of a very large number of people, mainly employees of the clients. The company had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures. It was fined RON 50,553, equal to EUR 10,000, for breaching Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR.

A former customer received a postal letter from CaixaBank concerning privacy policy updates and commercial profiling, despite having terminated their contractual relationship in 2008. The customer made an access request and then submitted a complaint to the AEPD. CaixaBank argued that retention was justified under Article 6(1)(b) GDPR based on an open credit line with a maturity date in 2030, but the AEPD found that the mortgage credit agreement had been formally cancelled in February 2008. Holding the complainant's data for almost 16 years without a valid purpose violated the storage limitation principle, and the AEPD imposed a fine of EUR 200,000 for infringing Article 5(1)(e) GDPR.
The DPA reprimanded a daycare center and its debt collection agency for unlawfully processing incorrect information about outstanding debt and failure to delete incorrect information.

The ICO investigated, jointly with the Canadian privacy regulator, a 2023 credential stuffing attack on the US genetic testing company 23andMe in which a threat actor accessed customer accounts and genetic and health data. It found that 23andMe failed to implement adequate authentication (such as mandatory MFA), extra protection for raw genetic data, preparation for credential stuffing, and effective monitoring and detection. These failures breached the UK GDPR security principle and Article 32. The ICO imposed a penalty of £2,310,000, set with regard to the company's significantly deteriorated financial position. By 31 December 2024 the infringements had been remedied, so no enforcement notice was given.

A complainant received numerous unsolicited promotional emails for the website noicompriamoauto.it, sent by third-party partners acting for the company, and had also not received a timely answer to his rights request. The Garante found the company to be the controller, that it had not properly regulated its relationships with the partners, had not supervised them, could not prove valid consent, and had made it hard to exercise rights. It imposed a fine of EUR 45,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were added because the company had ended the partner contracts and the email campaigns.

The DPA fined a consulting firm €21,000 for unintentionally disclosing personal data of numerous job applicants to the other applicants due to linking to an internal Google spreadsheet in the communication with the applicants. Thus, violating Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.

After an online inspection by the Guardia di Finanza of the e-commerce site confalonieriauto.it in November 2023, the Garante found that the site's cookie banner gave incomplete information, reappeared on every visit when users clicked the X, and had no warning that closing it leaves default settings in place. The cookie policy and privacy policy were also outdated. The company changed the banner during the proceeding, but the Garante found the changes still non-compliant. The Garante ordered the company to bring its cookie processing into line and issued a reprimand, with no fine.

The Italian DPA checked the website of Centralcar S.p.A. during online inspections carried out by the Guardia di Finanza in November 2023. The cookie banner had no close button or option to refuse, and it did not allow granular consent, so the consent it sought was not valid. The information in the short cookie notice was also found inadequate. The company changed the banner during the proceeding, and the DPA found that these changes restored compliance. It issued a reprimand (ammonimento) and no fine, and ordered the case to be recorded in its internal register.

The DPA found that a controller failed to respond to a data subject’s access request in time and failed to provide them with a full copy of their personal data, in violation of Article 12 and Article 15 GDPR.

The DPA fined a car rental company €100,000 for processing information about customers’ previous incidents in blacklists without a legal basis. Being blacklisted led to the denial of services by the rental company.

The Austrian DSB was running an ex officio investigation and asked the company three times to comment (14 June 2023, 3 August 2023 and 11 October 2024), each time pointing to its duty to cooperate under Art. 31 GDPR. The company never replied, and its managing director did not appear when the DSB summoned him for questioning (summons of 19 December 2024). The DSB fined the company EUR 16,000 under Art. 31 with Art. 83(4)(a) GDPR, finding intent and treating three earlier fines for breaches of Art. 31 as aggravating. The fine is not final: the company appealed to the Federal Administrative Court on 20 June 2025.

A data subject asked the controller, UAB Medical Score, on 2024-11-17 for a copy of his personal data and related information under Article 15 GDPR. The controller did not respond, because it had no record of him buying any product, and only later found that another person had carried out the transaction he cited. The Inspectorate held the complaint justified for breaches of Article 12(3) and Article 15(1) and (3) GDPR. It issued a reprimand and ordered the controller, by 2025-06-20, to grant the access right and to adopt suitable technical and organisational measures. No fine was imposed.
The DPA fined a company €3,000 for the use of non-essential cookies on their website without the user's prior consent and for two other cookie-related infractions.
The DPA fined a telecommunications company €200,000 for issuing a duplicate of a data subject’s SIM card to a third person without the knowledge or consent of the data subject.

This is the AEPD's ruling on the telecom operator DIGI's appeal for reconsideration (recurso de reposición) against the AEPD's resolution of 8 November 2024. That resolution fined DIGI EUR 200,000 for infringing Article 6(1) GDPR. A third party obtained a duplicate SIM card for the complainant at a DIGI point of sale on 6 April 2021, leaving the complainant without service. DIGI argued that it had followed its procedure, that it was being held strictly liable, that the fine was disproportionate, and that mitigating factors applied. The AEPD rejected every argument, found that no new facts or legal arguments had been raised, dismissed the appeal and left the EUR 200,000 fine in place.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation in April 2025 into an insurance broker that had notified a personal data breach after a cyber attack. Personal data of a significant number of clients, including national ID numbers, ID card photos, driving licences and contact details, was affected. The authority found that the broker had no security measures requiring secure access to its network storage equipment, so it had not ensured a level of security appropriate to the risk. It found a breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR and fined the broker RON 24,887 (about EUR 5,000).

The DPA fined an employer €42,000 for unlawfully adding a former employee’s personal mobile number to a WhatsApp group for employees after the employee explicitly opposed to use her private phone number for work-related communication.
The DPA imposed a €1,100,000 fine to an online pharmacy that made its customers identifiable by sharing their data with third-party tracking services.

The DPA fined an energy provider €1,380,000 for mistakenly attributing a data subject with another client’s gas supply contract and billing them based on the wrong contract, in violation of data accuracy and security of processing.

The DPA fined an electrical services company €10,000 for transferring the data subject's personal data to a grants management company without a valid legal basis. The former made a list of its customers available to a third party as part of an outsourcing arrangement.

The DPA fined Autostrade per l'Italia €420,000 for unlawfully processing an employee's personal data for disciplinary proceedings. The data included screenshots from the employee's social media account and private communications.
The DPA fined a telecommunications company €200,000 for issuing a duplicate e-SIM card to an unauthorised person without a valid legal basis.

The Italian DPA inspected Menarini Silicon Biosystems, which was extending an AI tool (CellFind) to classify multiple myeloma tumour cells, using pseudonymised patient data collected via a Bulgarian processor. The tool had first been trained for metastatic breast, prostate and colorectal tumours, mainly on data from a US group company. The DPA found breaches of transparency and the duty to give complete information, storage limitation and accountability. It accepted that the company had assessed the re-identification risk of that US data. It declared the processing unlawful and fined the company EUR 21,000. It ordered the company to state the necessary retention period, submit an amended privacy notice and report how it will publicise the notice. The decision is also published on the Garante's website.
The DPA ordered the provider of DeepSeek AI to appoint a representative in the EU, according to Article 27 GDPR.

A user of a screenshot-sharing software product, on a free account, asked the provider for a free copy of his screenshots after making access and portability requests under the GDPR. The provider gave his data but said the screenshots could only be exported with a paid licence, and the user complained. The Chamber found that the screenshots remained viewable through a URL, so the access right was served, and that the user was seeking a paid feature for free, which amounted to an abuse of rights. It dismissed the complaint without examining the merits and made no finding of infringement.
A building association was fined €1,000 for posting the minutes of their general assembly containing a list of debtors in the building lobby, in violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.

Romania's data protection authority investigated Maravet S.R.L. after it notified a personal data breach: a former employee copied personal data from the company's database without authorisation and posted it on the website of his new employer. The data of a significant number of people was exposed, including ID numbers, employee records and photos. The authority found the controller had not ensured that persons acting under its authority process data only on its instructions and had not implemented adequate technical and organisational security measures. It fined the controller RON 24,885.50 (about EUR 5,000), which has been paid.

The DPA fined a national credit bureau €200,000 for unlawfully including information regarding a data subject’s unpaid debt in their credit information system and not adequately responding to the data subject’s erasure requests.

ANSPDCP completed an investigation in April 2025 into an accounting and audit consulting company after it notified a personal data breach. Unauthorised persons had illegally accessed personal data of the employees of the company's clients. The authority found that the controller had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures, contrary to Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It imposed a fine of 24,887 lei (about EUR 5,000) and a corrective measure under Article 58(2)(d) to periodically check compliance with data protection procedures and to train staff. The controller has paid the fine.

The Council's response to a Freedom of Information request, published in October 2021, was a spreadsheet containing 35 hidden workbooks, and personal data was hidden in 10 of them. The data of 6,528 people was exposed, including 2,342 children in care, 96 of them unaccompanied asylum-seeking children. The platform WhatDoTheyKnow told the Council in November 2023, and the Council and the platform then removed the response. The ICO found the Council lacked adequate measures to check spreadsheets for hidden data and issued a reprimand, citing the remedial steps the Council had taken.

The CNIL inspected Solocal Marketing Services, a direct-marketing subsidiary of the Solocal group, in October 2022. The company ran email and SMS prospecting campaigns for clients and passed prospect data to clients for postal and telephone marketing, all from a database of about 75 million entries covering some 35 million people. The restricted committee found breaches of Article L. 34-5 of the postal and electronic communications code (consent for electronic prospecting) and of Article 7 GDPR (proof of consent). It also noted a lack of legal basis under Article 6 for part of the data transmitted, but fined only for L. 34-5 CPCE and Article 7. It imposed a fine of EUR 900,000, an injunction to stop electronic prospecting without valid consent with a EUR 10,000 daily penalty after nine months, and publication of the decision, with the company no longer named after two years.

CALOGA, a data broker and e-mail prospecting company holding four prospect databases of over 2.8 million people, was inspected by the CNIL in May 2022. The restricted committee found breaches of Articles 5(1)(e) and 6 GDPR and of Article L. 34-5 of the postal and electronic communications code, because prospecting and transfers of data to partners took place without valid consent or a valid legal basis. The alleged breach of Article 32 (security) was not upheld. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 80,000, taking account of the company's cessation of activity and financial situation, and ordered publication, with the company no longer identifiable after two years.
The DPA clarified that direct marketing and political advertising are distinct and incompatible purposes for processing personal data, and warned a politician over unlawful political advertising.

The Romanian DPA closed an investigation in April 2025 into a tax and finance company that had notified a personal data breach. A cyber attack gave unauthorised access to the data of a significant number of employees of the company's clients and locked the company out of its own IT infrastructure. The authority found that the company had not put appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place, in breach of Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It fined the company RON 9,954.80 (about EUR 2,000) and ordered periodic checks of its data protection procedures and regular staff training. The company has paid the fine.

The Romanian data protection authority investigated Romoffice Construct Holding Ag SRL after a complaint from an individual. The company used the complainant's phone number, given when filling in an online form to apply for a public funding programme, to call him about a promotional campaign. It could not show a legal basis for this processing. The authority found breaches of the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle and of accountability, read with Article 6(1), and fined the company RON 9,954 (about EUR 2,000).

A job candidate complained that a logistics company required a criminal record certificate for a job interview and handed out a form asking for marital status and number of children. The company argued that air-security rules required the certificate and that the form data was needed for tax withholding (Modelo 145). The AEPD found that both requests were excessive for candidates with no employment relationship and breached the data minimisation principle. It imposed two fines under Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, EUR 75,000 and EUR 25,000, and rejected the request for a mere reprimand.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in April 2025 into CV PRO CONSULT S.R.L., which had notified a personal data breach. A cyber attack gave unauthorised access to the personal data of many employees of the company's clients and locked the company out of its own IT infrastructure. The authority found that the company had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures under Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It fined the company RON 9,955 (about EUR 2,000) and ordered periodic checks of its data protection procedures and regular training of staff. The company has paid the fine.

A person who had been listed in the ASNEF credit information file as guarantor of a mortgage loan complained to the AEPD after a court ruling showed the debt was not owed. The AEPD found the controller, CREDIFIMO, had no legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR for keeping and reporting the data, and proposed a fine of EUR 200,000 and an order to delete the data from ASNEF. CREDIFIMO admitted liability and paid voluntarily, taking two cumulative 20% reductions, so the fine became EUR 120,000 and the procedure was closed.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation of ROUMASPORT SRL in April 2025, started after complaints. The company accessed the video surveillance system at one of its work points and unlawfully processed images of its employees, including for disciplinary investigations. It was found to have breached Articles 5(1)(a) and (b) and 6(1) GDPR and was fined 24,887 lei (about EUR 5,000). It was also ordered to bring video monitoring into compliance, especially for disciplinary investigations.

IMY supervised the visa work of the Swedish Consulate General in Istanbul, including the outsourced applicant-intake provider VFS Global, after an on-site inspection in March 2024. It found that the consulate processed personal data in breach of Article 28(1) and Article 32(1) GDPR, because it did not ensure that the processor's fingerprint capture and handling of passports were adequately secured. IMY imposed no fine, judging the deficiencies not serious enough, but ordered the consulate to submit an action plan within three months after the decision becomes final.

The Irish DPC announced its final decision following an inquiry into TikTok's transfers of EEA users' personal data to China, including remote access by staff there, and the transparency of its privacy policy about those transfers. It found that TikTok infringed Article 46(1) GDPR because it did not verify, guarantee and demonstrate essentially equivalent protection, and Article 13(1)(f) GDPR because its 2021 privacy policy did not name the third countries or explain the processing. It imposed fines totalling €530 million (€485 million and €45 million) and ordered TikTok to bring its processing into compliance within 6 months, failing which transfers to China are to be suspended. The DPC also noted that TikTok later reported that some EEA data had in fact been stored on servers in China, contrary to its evidence, and is considering further action.

The CNPD opened an investigation into a Luxembourg engineering company to check compliance with Article 30 GDPR on the record of processing activities. It found that the record was incomplete (missing controller/DPO details, descriptions of data categories and erasure time limits), a breach of Article 30(1)(a), (c) and (f). Treating it as a single, low-gravity infringement under Article 83(4), the restricted panel imposed an administrative fine of EUR 7,000. It declined to order corrective measures because the company had fixed its record after the statement of objections.

A complaint said the Municipality of Patra had published on its official website a post about a school committee member, including his name, workplace, job position and political beliefs, plus an extract of an email he had sent to the other committee members before a meeting. The post was later removed from the website. The Authority held that the publication breached the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, rejected the municipality's journalistic and public-interest arguments, and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000. The Authority examined the case in its session of 15 January 2025; the decision document is dated 30 April 2025.

The Order of Psychologists of Lombardy notified a ransomware attack in October 2023 by the NoEscape group, in which data were encrypted, exfiltrated and published on the dark web. About 3,000 people and about 15,000 records were affected, including special-category data, criminal-offence data and data covered by professional secrecy. The Garante found that the Order had not put in place adequate measures to detect breaches promptly and to secure the data, in breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1). It fined the Order EUR 30,000 as a single fine for the combined infringement, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ceased and new measures had been adopted.

The Italian DPA inspected the Lombardy Region on its own initiative regarding processing of employee data at work, including remote work. It found unlawful processing of email metadata, internet browsing logs and data in the old OTRS ticketing system, involving breaches of lawfulness, minimisation, storage limitation, data protection by design, DPIA, processor contract and employment-specific rules. It ordered corrective measures on browsing logs within 90 days and imposed separate fines of EUR 20,000, 25,000 and 5,000, totalling EUR 50,000, with publication.

A real estate agency received unsolicited marketing contacts by WhatsApp and phone from phone numbers it had bought from a data supplier, Realmaps. The agency could not show that the data subjects had been given notice or had consented, and it sent data subject requests back to the supplier instead of handling them itself. The Garante found breaches of the GDPR principles, lawfulness, information, accountability and data subject rights, and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000. It also ordered the agency to adopt verification procedures and rights-handling measures, and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.
The DPA fined a real estate agency €40,000 for unlawfully processing personal data for direct marketing and for failing to adequately respond to an access request.

A data subject complained that a hospital, Tirrenia Hospital S.r.l., did not answer his access request under Article 15 GDPR. The hospital only replied after the Garante invited it to comply. It blamed a hard-disk failure on the computer used to receive certified emails, but the Garante found the delay was caused by negligent conduct by the controller. The Garante found a breach of Article 12 in relation to Article 15 and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000, with an order to publish the injunction on its website.

The Garante investigated an energy supplier after numerous complaints about unsolicited telemarketing calls, including to numbers on the public opposition register, and about missing replies to data subject rights requests. It found that the company answered the Authority's information requests inadequately and late, failed to identify roles in its sales network (controller/processor), had no valid legal basis or consent for the calls, and mishandled rights requests. It fined the company EUR 100,000, imposed corrective orders including a ban on further processing of the complainants' data, and ordered publication of the decision.

A complaint alleged that a social cooperative, which runs school services for the Municipality of Bologna, emailed the municipality an Excel file with sheets listing children with disabilities and special needs, including their conditions, after an employee's mistake in a strike notice. The Garante found that the cooperative, acting as processor, breached Articles 28(3) and 32(1) GDPR by sending special-category data of vulnerable minors without adequate technical and organisational measures and contrary to the controller's instructions. It fined the cooperative EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed because the conduct had ceased to have effect.

Ten people who had brought an appeal before the administrative court against the municipality complained that their personal data were published online. The municipality had put a council resolution and its annexes on its website, including names, initials, dates of birth, addresses and tax codes of the appellants. The Garante found that no transparency rule required publishing these data, that the data minimisation principle was breached and that the data stayed online beyond the 15-day period. It fined the municipality EUR 1,200 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the data had been removed.

A cooperative working for the Municipality of Bologna sent an email about a strike with an Excel file that accidentally still contained health and disability data of about 60 children in municipal nursery schools. The municipal office forwarded it to all the schools, coordinators and territorial managers, and one school sent it on to 53 parent email addresses. The Garante found that the Municipality processed special-category data without a lawful basis, in breach of Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and the Italian Code. It fined the Municipality EUR 40,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures because the conduct had ended.

The Garante investigated the cookie practices of a company's website (its name is withheld in the decision) after a Guardia di Finanza audit on 8 November 2023. The cookie banner gave generic information, its choices disappeared after one click, and the links to the privacy and cookie policies did not work, so consent for non-technical cookies was not valid. During the proceedings the company updated its privacy notices and reconfigured the banner. The Garante considered these measures adequate, imposed no further corrective measures and no fine, and issued a reprimand (ammonimento).

A person whose name appears in search results linked to a 2020 plea-bargained criminal conviction for economic and extortion-related offences complained to the Garante about Google's refusal to delist eight news URLs. Google had already delisted four of them in EU versions. The Garante rejected the complaint for two URLs (6 and 8), which it found current and of public interest, and upheld it for URLs 2 and 5, ordering Google to remove them from name-based search results within twenty days. No fine was imposed.

A public official complained to the Garante about an article by MF Service S.r.l. reporting a house-arrest measure against him, which a court had later revoked. He asked for the article to be deindexed and for its headline to be corrected under Article 16 GDPR. The publisher added a note in the headline, body and URL about the revocation, but refused to deindex, citing public interest and ongoing criminal proceedings. The Garante held that Article 16 covers only objectively inaccurate data, found none, and considered the update under Article 5(1)(d) fully satisfied; it declared the deindexing complaint unfounded and took no further measures.

The Swiss FDPIC investigated a debt collection company that published names, addresses, photos and other personal data of alleged debtors and people connected to them (including family members and children) on a website, asking visitors to report their whereabouts. The investigation began after a complaint forwarded by the Bavarian authority. The FDPIC found breaches of the transparency and proportionality principles with no overriding private or public interest. It ordered the company to stop publishing such data, delete what was already published, and report the deletion within 10 days of the decision becoming final. No fine was imposed; only an administrative fee of CHF 3,200 was charged. The decision has been appealed to the Federal Administrative Court and is not yet final.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation into Xiting ROM SRL in April 2025 after a complaint from an individual. The company had not given the complainant a proper and complete written answer within the legal time limit to her access request, which asked for information on the processing of her data and an electronic copy. The authority found breaches of Article 12(3)-(4) with Article 15(1)-(3) GDPR and fined the company RON 4,977 (about EUR 1,000). It also ordered corrective measures: a full reply to the complainant and compliance measures, including staff training, for handling data subject requests.

IMY examined a complaint that Aller Media AB processed a complainant's personal data through cookies on its website recept.se on 21 May 2021 without a legal basis. Aller relied on legitimate interest alongside consent, and IMY found it had not shown that legitimate interest could justify the processing. IMY found a violation of Article 6(1)(f) GDPR but issued a reprimand rather than a fine, treating it as a minor infringement given the changes Aller made after supervision began and its lack of prior violations. The complainant's other objections about the cookie banner design were not examined.

Following complaints, the Romanian DPA investigated a travel company that published on its Facebook page a table of tourists' personal data (names, booking numbers, hotel/location, stay dates) for a prize draw. It found inadequate security measures, failure to notify the personal data breach, and no proof of a full reply to access requests. It fined the company EUR 5,000 for Art. 32 and EUR 1,000 for Art. 33, issued a warning for Art. 15 with Art. 12(3)-(4), and ordered corrective measures on security, breach handling and answering the access request.

The DPA reprimanded a retail company, as well as its data supplier, for unlawfully processing the potential customers’ personal data for direct marketing purposes without having verified the lawfulness of the initial collection. The controller was therefore unable to demonstrate an overriding legitimate interest.

The DPA assessed the FATCA agreement and held that it is not compatible with the GDPR. It reprimanded the Public Federal Service of Finances over several GDPR violations and ordered it to bring its disclosures under FATCA into compliance.

In decision 172/2022 the Belgian Litigation Chamber had ordered a real estate agency to remedy several GDPR infringements and warned it about publishing location data of sold properties. The agency did not appeal or request a hearing on the merits but only partly complied, deliberately keeping some elements online for over two years. The Chamber found non-compliance with the order, punishable under Article 83(6) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 6,000, calculated from a starting point of EUR 5,000 for a one-person company and raised by 20% because the agency persistently refused to give its current turnover.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in April 2025 into Dante International SA after a customer complained about the processing of email addresses linked to their account on the company's online platform. Although the company confirmed the addresses had been deleted, the complainant still received a feedback message at them, and some of the company's collaborators could view or use the address. The company did not handle the repeated erasure requests properly and gave no clear, transparent information. It was fined 49,770 lei (about EUR 10,000) and ordered to answer the complainant and put technical and organisational measures in place.

The Swedish DPA IMY examined a regional hospital board in Uppsala after a personal data incident was reported in November 2022. Patient data, including personal identity numbers and health data, had been sent by unencrypted email and stored in Microsoft Outlook from 2010 to 2022. IMY found that the controller did not take appropriate technical and organisational measures to prevent and detect unauthorised processing of patient data in its email service, in breach of Article 32(1) GDPR for the period from 25 May 2018 to 29 November 2022. Considering the circumstances, including a prior IMY decision against the same controller, IMY found a fine disproportionate and issued a reprimand instead.

The DPA warned the Belgian Post Group for violating the principle of data minimisation. The DPA clarified that the principle applies even when the means of the data processing are explicitly provided for by national law.

The Equality Ombudsman (DO) ran a web form for tips and complaints about discrimination. An analytics tool from a processor was meant to mask free-text entries, but the masking did not work on the form's summary page. Personal data, some of it sensitive or covered by secrecy, was therefore transferred to and stored with the processor for about a year (1 Sept 2020 to 17 Sept 2021). IMY found that DO had not taken appropriate technical and organisational measures under Article 32(1). It rejected a reprimand as too lenient, rated the infringement as low severity, found no aggravating or mitigating factors, and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 100,000.

A complainant, passed on by the Finnish data protection authority under the Article 60 cooperation procedure, objected that the company Y required a customer account before a complaint about its service could be filed. The Belgian APD Litigation Chamber found that the Finnish website's complaint page made an account necessary, which could breach Article 25 read with Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. Because Y had since added a guest option for complaints in the Finnish site, the Chamber issued a warning under Article 58(2)(a) on a prima facie basis, not a fine.

A business manager received direct marketing from a company that had obtained his data from a data broker. He then sent the broker an access request and objected to the processing. The Litigation Chamber found that the broker had no demonstrated legal basis for the processing, did not proactively inform the data subjects, and handled the access request incompletely. It ordered compliance with the access request, erasure of data without a lawful basis, notification of recipients and proactive information. It imposed three fines of EUR 8,000, 6,000 and 6,000 (total EUR 20,000). The Market Court later partly annulled the decision and reduced the fines.
A store was fined €12,000 for failing to implement appropriate access restrictions regarding CCTV footage, in violation of Article 32 GDPR.
The Belgian DPA reprimanded a school for infractions on Article 5.1(a), Article 6.1(e), Article 9.2(a) and clarified the interpretation of Article 8.
The DPA fined a telecommunications company €200,000 for duplicating a data subject's SIM card for a third person without the knowledge or consent of the data subject.

In November 2022 police found ten boxes of a funeral home's documents by a road; they contained 82 authorisations with personal data of relatives of deceased persons. The boxes had fallen off the open bed of a vehicle during transport and had previously been kept in an unlocked room. The President of UODO found that the controller did not carry out a proper risk analysis, could not show accountability, and did not report the breach to the authority. He imposed a fine of PLN 33,000 and ordered measures to minimise risks within 30 days.
The operator of a mobile application was fined €600 for requiring users to upload a copy of the ID card to attain “verified” status on the platform, in violation of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

The Romanian authority investigated United Business Solutions SRL after a guest complained that, following an accommodation service, the company sent a fiscal document containing his personal data by email to a third party without his consent. The investigation found that the company had not implemented sufficient technical and organisational measures to protect client data confidentiality, and had not ensured that persons acting under its authority processed data only on its instructions. The company was fined 9,954 lei (stated as the equivalent of EUR 2,000) and ordered to revise its internal procedures and train staff periodically.

The AEPD investigated CAMERDATA after an association complained that the data of self-employed people (name, tax ID, address, phone, email) taken from the Chambers of Commerce census was being exposed and sold online. It found that CAMERDATA had no legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR for processing these data. It also found that CAMERDATA did not inform the individuals as Article 14 GDPR requires, and it rejected the 'disproportionate effort' exemption and the general notice on chamber websites. It fined CAMERDATA EUR 200,000 for Article 6(1) and EUR 60,000 for Article 14, and archived the charges about the transfer to KOMPASS and about Article 28. It ordered deletion of the data from the Chamber of Commerce transfer, a halt to processing until a legal basis exists, and individual information to the people concerned.
The DPA fined the Spanish Chamber of Commerce €500,000 for transferring self-employed persons’ tax identity numbers to private companies without a legal basis.

A complaint alleged that data of self-employed persons taken from the AEAT economic activities census were passed to the Chambers of Commerce, CAMERDATA and private companies, and published and used for marketing without proper information. The AEPD found that INFORMA D&B processed the data obtained from CAMERDATA without a valid legal basis (legitimate interest not established) and did not meet the duty to inform data subjects under Article 14. It rejected the company's arguments on nullity, disproportionality and change of criteria, and its claim that one offence was only the means of committing the other. It imposed two fines of EUR 900,000 each (EUR 1.8 million in total) and ordered the company to stop processing the data obtained under the CAMERDATA contract until it has a legal basis, and to delete the data.
The DPA fined a marketing company €42,000 for processing personal data of self-employed persons originating from the Spanish Chamber of Commerce without a legal basis.

DPP Law Ltd, a English law firm, suffered a cyber incident in which the personal data of 791 clients and expert witnesses was taken and posted on the dark web. The Commissioner found that DPP lacked appropriate security (it did not apply least privilege and did not audit administrative accounts) and notified the breach 43 days late. He found infringements of Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1), 32(2) and 33(1) UK GDPR and imposed a single penalty of £60,000.

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation in March 2025 into Office Nova Concept SRL after an individual complained that the company had installed cameras pointed at the entrance to their home without consent. The data subject had asked by email for the cameras to be redirected and for images of people using the entrance to be deleted. The company did not send a proper written reply within the legal deadline, which breached Article 12(1)-(4) read with Articles 21 and 17 GDPR. The authority fined the company 4,977.4 lei (about EUR 1,000) and ordered corrective measures: a proper reply to the request, compliance of its request-handling and transparency practices, and cameras that no longer capture the complainant's property.

The DPA fined a company that buys outstanding loans from banks €200,000 for unlawfully including a data subject’s debt in a public credit registry, with the knowledge that said debt had been exonerated two years before in the course of insolvency procedures.

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation in March 2025 into a gambling company that had notified a personal data breach. A cyber attack let a third party access employee data held in the company's IT infrastructure. The authority found that the company had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures and had not regularly tested and evaluated their effectiveness. It fined the company RON 9,951.20, equivalent to EUR 2,000, under Article 32. The company has already paid the fine.

The DPA fined the provider of the “virtual companion” Replika AI €5,000,000 for unlawfully processing personal data, for transparency violations, and for failing to implement effective age verification mechanisms.

Following a report by a TV journalist, the Garante and the Guardia di finanza inspected a network of unauthorised call centres that sold Acea Energia energy contracts using illicitly obtained 'switch-out' contact lists and misleading calls, channelling contracts through an Acea-contracted agency. The Garante found that Acea had allowed promotional calls without consent or information, had de facto entrusted data to a company without a processor appointment, let its staff access Acea systems without designation, and failed to supervise its sales chain. It fined Acea EUR 3,000,000, ordered it to inform all affected data subjects and to check that agencies' sub-agent contracts comply with Article 28, and ordered publication of the decision.

Following a report by a TV journalist, the Garante and the Guardia di Finanza inspected several call centres and agencies selling Acea Energia energy contracts. They found huge purchased contact lists used for promotional calls without valid consent or information notices, missing processor designations under Article 28, unauthorised access to Acea's systems, and in one case incomplete cooperation with the Authority. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, banned the use of the lists found and of any contact lists whose lawfulness cannot be proven, and ordered the five entities to report back within 30 days. It fined them EUR 45,000, 200,000, 500,000, 75,000 and 30,000 (EUR 850,000 in total) and ordered publication of the decision.

A man complained about an unwanted promotional phone call from a real estate agency, which had obtained his contact data from a list broker (Realmaps). The Garante found that the agency, as controller, had not verified or documented consent or information given to the data subjects, had not checked the Public Opposition Register, used a call script lacking Article 13 information, and redirected rights requests to the supplier. It banned further marketing use of the lists, ordered deletion and compliance measures, and fined the agency EUR 15,000.

An employee of the Unione Montana Appennino Parma Est complained about a video surveillance camera at the entrance of the local police command, filmed 24/7 and recorded. The Garante found that the camera, which also films workers, was installed without a union agreement or labour inspectorate authorisation, and that its 'integrated urban security' justification was irrelevant. It also found transparency failings (information notices) and no data protection impact assessment for workers' data. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, fined the Unione EUR 8,000 and ordered it to correct the first-level information sign. The decision is to be published.

Employees of a small municipality complained that individual performance evaluations, with names and scores, were published on the municipality's online notice board and website. The Garante found that about 40 employees' names and scores were disseminated online for 15 days without a suitable legal basis. Neither the municipal regulation, Art. 124 of the local government code nor the transparency decree required named publication; the transparency decree requires only aggregated data. The Garante found a breach of Articles 5 and 6 GDPR and Art. 2-ter of the Code and fined the municipality EUR 4,000, ordering publication of the order on its website. No further corrective measures were needed as the content had been removed.

An estate agency, Undici S.r.l.s., made promotional telephone calls using about 20,881 phone numbers bought from a data supplier (Realmaps), without verifying or documenting consent or the information given to the data subjects, and without checking the Public Opposition Register. It also handled data subjects' requests poorly, depending on the supplier to answer them, and could not show accountability. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, ordered corrective measures and imposed a fine of EUR 8,000, and ordered publication of the decision.

Following a complaint, the Romanian authority investigated Tensa Art Design S.A., owner of the lensa.ro website, which sent marketing SMS messages to the complainant's phone number without proof of consent. The company also failed to handle the complainant's access and erasure requests properly. It was fined RON 49,774 (EUR 10,000) for the lack of a legal basis and RON 24,887 (EUR 5,000) for breaching the data subject rights provisions. Corrective measures were also ordered.

The Garante learned from a press article that AMAT, a company wholly owned by the City of Milan (AMAT's own statement to the Garante) and treated by the Garante as a private-law company, had installed two AI-equipped cameras in Milan to count traffic and pedestrians. It found that the footage, even with faces and number plates blurred, was still personal data, that the privacy notices were inaccurate and incomplete (wrongly claiming anonymisation, missing retention and legal basis, a general second-level notice), that no dated DPIA was proven before processing started, and that the DPO was put in a conflict of interest by being asked to draft and sign the DPIA. The Garante dropped its legal-basis charge after AMAT's defence; AMAT relied on legitimate interest. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and fined AMAT EUR 9,000, with the decision published, and ordered no further corrective measures.

A patient complained against her former private gynaecologist, alleging incomplete access to her medical file, repeated unauthorised access to her electronic health record on the national eHealth platform after the doctor-patient relationship ended, and disclosure of her health data to third parties. The Authority found that the doctor deliberately and repeatedly processed the complainant's health data unlawfully between October 2021 and May 2022, in breach of the lawfulness principle of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83(5)(a) GDPR.
An online store operator was fined €3000 after two customer email complaints were merged, revealing their personal data to each other respectively, in violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.

The DPA dismissed the internal appeal of a utilities company and imposed a €200,000 fine for unlawfully transferring data on the data subject’s debt to a credit information agency without informing the data subject prior to the transfer.
The DPA fined a telecommunications company €70,000 for providing inaccurate data in the course of an investigation related to unwanted advertising calls to a data subject.

A complainant said a bank branch employee had signed a data protection and economic activity form in his name, and in his wife's name, for a mortgage enquiry without their consent, and that the marketing and profiling consent boxes were ticked. The AEPD opened a sanctioning procedure against BBVA for breach of the lawfulness principle in Article 6(1) GDPR, with a proposed fine of 200,000 euros. BBVA acknowledged responsibility and paid voluntarily, qualifying for two cumulative 20% reductions. The AEPD terminated the procedure with a reduced fine of 120,000 euros.

A data subject complained that the Employment Service did not answer their access request within one month; the reply came on 2024-10-14. The authority found the one-month deadline under Article 12(3) GDPR was missed, because the controller did not inform the data subject of the extension or the reasons for the delay. The part of the complaint about disclosing the names of the recipients of the data (Article 15(1)(c) GDPR) was dismissed. The controller received a reprimand.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation of Banca Transilvania in March 2025 after a complaint from an individual. The complainant's mortgage had been paid off, yet a new natural-disaster insurance policy was wrongly issued with an insurer acting for the bank, without consent. The bank had also wrongly requested a significant number of policies, using customers' personal data. The authority found a breach of the lawfulness and fairness principle and the lack of a legal basis, fined the bank 24,883 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to bring its data collection and further processing into compliance.
A restaurant was fined €500 after unlawfully adding over 200 people to a WhatsApp group to advertise their New Years Eve party without their consent.
The DPA issued a warning to the administrator of a website for refusing to provide the DPA with a list of the persons who followed a user’s profile on the website.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in March 2025 into BINBOX GLOBAL SERVICES S.R.L., started after the company notified a personal data breach. A cyber attack accessed and encrypted the company's IT infrastructure, leading to unauthorised disclosure of or access to the data of a significant number of its customers. The authority found the company had not applied appropriate technical and organisational measures and breached Article 32(1)(b), (d) and 32(2) GDPR. It fined the company RON 14,930.70 (EUR 3,000), which the company has already paid.

A patient complained to the Maltese Commissioner that a hospital kept an old residential address for her, which she had left in 2006, despite her asking for it to be corrected. As a result, her histopathology reports were sent to third parties at that address. The hospital had also obtained her data from the Electoral Register without telling her and without a lawful basis, and had not appointed a data protection officer. The Commissioner found infringements of the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principles, the accuracy principle, the right to rectification and the duty to designate a DPO. He ordered the hospital to rectify the data, erase other data subjects' data taken from the Electoral Register and appoint a DPO. He also imposed three administrative fines totalling EUR 20,000.

The DPA held that a hospital manager who consults their subordinate's medical file in excess of its internal competences acts as controller for this processing and not the hospital. However, the hospital failed to notify the data breach to the DPA.
The DPA fined a telecommunications company €20,000 for sending a data subject direct marketing without their consent.

On 11 April 2023 Mad Cool launched a web form for ticket holders to confirm their postal details for festival wristbands. The same morning the platform had been moved to a new server with a 2-second micro-cache left active, so for a short time some users saw other users' personal data. The AEPD received six complaints and opened sanction proceedings. It found a breach of the confidentiality principle (Art. 5(1)(f)) and of the security obligation (Art. 32, including the absence of a VPN). It set fines of EUR 2,000 and EUR 1,500, totalling EUR 3,500. The company paid early and waived any administrative appeal (a court challenge remained open), so a 20% reduction applied and the amount paid was EUR 2,800.

Two people complained, one of them a complainant in a workplace harassment investigation, that the company had disclosed the identities of complainants and accused. The company sent the investigation resolutions, naming complainants and accused, to 15 people. The AEPD found a breach of the confidentiality principle in Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. The company admitted responsibility and paid early, so the proposed 200,000 euro fine was reduced by two 20% reductions to 120,000 euros. The AEPD also ordered the company to tell it, within 3 months of the decision becoming final and enforceable, which confidentiality measures it had adopted.

A real estate agency was fined €12,000 after requiring their employees to take photos of mailboxes so that details of the property owners could be included in a database, in violation of Article 6(1) & 14 GDPR.

The Garante found that the Municipality of Palma di Montechiaro had not designated a data protection officer (DPO), and had not published or communicated the DPO's contact details, until after proceedings were opened following its own checks. The municipality's later steps did not prevent a finding of breach. The Garante declared the conduct unlawful under Article 37(1) and (7) GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 3,000, with publication of the order and decision on its website and an entry in its internal register. No corrective measure was ordered because the municipality had already complied.

Three employees complained, via their lawyer, about a school's attendance system for administrative staff that used fingerprints combined with a badge. The Garante found that processing biometric data to record attendance had no legal basis, since the 2019 law providing for it had been repealed, and that employee consent cannot cure this given the imbalance in employment. The school had stopped the system and deleted the biometric data, so no further corrective measures were ordered. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 4,000, with publication.
A controller was fined £90,000 (€105,412.95) for making over 95,000 unsolicited marketing calls to numbers on a do-not-call list, in violation of national electronic communication legislation.

A ransomware attacker accessed the health and care IT environment of Advanced's AHC division in August 2022 and exfiltrated personal data, including health data, of tens of thousands of people, and healthcare services were disrupted. The ICO found that Advanced, as a processor, failed to implement appropriate security measures under Article 32(1) UK GDPR, with gaps in vulnerability scanning, patch management and multi-factor authentication. It rated the infringement highly serious and negligent, and treated the company's size and responsibility as aggravating, while its incident response and reporting to the NCSC were mitigating. A proposed penalty of £6.09 million was reached, then a settlement gave a 20% reduction and a final penalty of £3,076,320. Advanced agreed not to appeal.

After a cyber attack on NTT DATA Romania's IT infrastructure, personal data of a significant number of people was extracted without authorisation. The authority found the company had not implemented adequate technical and organisational security measures nor regularly tested their effectiveness. It also found the company failed to notify the authority within 72 hours. It fined the company RON 124,432.50 (EUR 25,000) for the security breach and issued a warning for the late notification. The company has paid the fine.
A delivery company was fined €70,000 for delivering a parcel to a third party resulting in the improper disclosure of personal data.

A press release from the Croatian DPA announcing seven fines totalling EUR 169,000. The part relevant to this record concerns a company that used its access to the Ministry of Interior's vehicle registry, granted for another purpose and city, to collect owners' data for parking fee collection for retail chains and a general hospital, without a legal basis. It also had no processor contract with the hospital and failed to take appropriate security measures. The Agency imposed a fine of EUR 80,000 on the company.

This is a press release summarising seven fines totalling EUR 169,000 issued by the Croatian DPA. The part matching this Fino entry concerns a company that publicly published data on craftsmen online, collected from public registers and financial data obtained under a contract. The Agency found no proven legal basis for publishing the data or keeping data of deregistered craftsmen permanently, a lack of transparency, a deficient record of processing activities and a data protection officer with a conflict of interest (also the director). It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 40,000.

The press release summarises seven fines issued by the Croatian DPA totalling EUR 169,000. The part relevant to this entry concerns the Clinical Hospital Centre Zagreb, which suffered a cyber attack after an attacker, probably using social engineering, gained VPN access and used an outdated operating system to obtain domain admin rights, copying at least 3 GB of data over 7 days. The Agency found insufficient technical security measures and multiple failings in system design (access restriction, monitoring, reporting, timely reaction), and imposed a fine of EUR 20,000.

A press release of 24 March 2025 summarising seven administrative fines totalling EUR 169,000 issued by the Croatian DPA. The part relevant to this record concerns General Hospital Zadar, which used a company's application that automatically pulled vehicle owners' data from the Ministry of Interior web service without a legal basis to issue daily parking tickets. The hospital also failed to inform parking users properly, did not take appropriate organisational measures, and had no processing contract with the company as processor. A fine of EUR 4,000 was imposed. The same release covers other fines (parking company, data publisher, KBC Zagreb, Vinkovci hospital, a casino and an oil producer) that are not part of this record.

This is a press release from the Croatian DPA announcing seven new administrative fines totalling EUR 169,000. Only a short passage concerns the casino: it and an oil and fat producer were fined for failing to comply with the GDPR rules on appointing and positioning a data protection officer. The casino received EUR 12,000 and the producer EUR 10,000. The other fines in the release (parking data, public disclosure of data, hospitals) are separate cases.

A press release from the Croatian DPA announces seven new administrative fines totalling EUR 169,000. This record concerns one of them: a fine of EUR 10,000 on an oil and fat manufacturing company for failing to comply with the rules on appointing and positioning a data protection officer. A casino received a EUR 12,000 fine for the same type of issue. The release gives no further detail on the oil and fat company's case.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in January 2025 into a hotel company after a complaint. A data subject had asked for all personal data held about them, including a copy of a signed document and any audio-video recording. The controller could not show it answered within the legal time limit, and its late answer, sent only after the authority intervened, did not give all the data. The authority found breaches of Articles 12(3), 13 and 15 GDPR, fined the company RON 4,975 (about EUR 1,000) and ordered corrective measures.

The DPA fined a real estate investor two fines of RON 4,977 each (EUR 2,000 in all) for failing to prove consent to the use of personal data for telemarketing, and for failing to respond to data access requests.
A DPA held that a controller processed a former employee's personal data unlawfully by redirecting the emails sent to their old work email account to another account.

A complainant alleged that the Chief Commander of the Police disclosed her personal data at a press conference, including health information, details of her private life and housing. The UODO President found that the disclosure of relationship, residence and housing data lacked a legal basis under Article 6(1) and that the disclosure of health data breached Article 9(1). He found the infringement intentional and serious, noting earlier violations by the Commander, and found no mitigating factors. An administrative fine of PLN 75,000 was imposed, close to the PLN 100,000 statutory cap for public finance units. The proceedings were discontinued as to one item of information that the press conference was found not to have disclosed.
A football club was fined €600 after disposing of a large number of documents in a bin on a public road. The documents contained the personal data of minors playing for the club.

The DPA fined the Polish Minister of Digitalisation PLN 100,000 (€23,448,50) and the Polish Post S.A. PLN 27,124,816 (€6,444,174) for unlawfully processing the personal data of ca. 30 million citizens in order to facilitate postal voting in a general election.

The UODO President opened proceedings of its own motion over the disclosure of data from the PESEL population register on 22 April 2020 to a state-owned postal company, for the planned postal-vote presidential election. It found that the Minister of Digital Affairs disclosed the data of all adult Polish citizens (PESEL number, names, addresses) without a legal basis, breaching Article 6(1) and the lawfulness principle in Article 5(1)(a). It fined the Minister PLN 100,000, the statutory maximum for public bodies. The same decision found the postal company processed the data unlawfully and fined it PLN 27,124,816. Only the Minister's part is summarised here.
The DPA fined a bank €1,600,000 for attempting to verify the origin of funds to be deposited by a prospective customer without a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR.

Carrefour notified the Spanish authority of five personal data breaches in which attackers gained unauthorised access to customer accounts on its website and the MiCarrefour app. The AEPD found that Carrefour breached the integrity and confidentiality principle (Art. 5(1)(f)), failed to apply adequate security measures (Art. 32) and failed to properly notify affected individuals (Art. 34). It imposed fines of EUR 2,000,000, EUR 1,000,000 and EUR 200,000 respectively, a total of EUR 3,200,000. It also ordered Carrefour to communicate the breaches to the affected individuals within one month of the decision becoming final. Carrefour accepted responsibility only for the Art. 34 infringement and asked for reductions, but these were not applied because it neither paid nor waived appeals.

A man started an online Vodafone fixed-line offer and abandoned it. A Vodafone dealer phoned him, got him to send his ID document via WhatsApp and used it to register a different activation in Vodafone's systems. The Garante found the dealer had exceeded its role as processor and acted as an autonomous controller without a legal basis, consent or privacy notice. It banned further processing of the complainant's data and fined the dealer EUR 15,000, with publication of the order.

A parent complained that the school had published on its YouTube channel a Christmas greetings video showing her son's class, including him, without her consent. The school said the boy had told teachers he was 14 and had agreed to appear, but he turned 14 only eleven days later. The Garante found that publishing the video had no valid legal basis for a public body, breaching GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 and Article 2-ter of the Italian Privacy Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

Three former employees of a bankrupt company complained that Encore Thermoengineering, which bought part of the business together with its email domain and servers, kept their individual mailboxes active, redirected incoming mail to its managing director and refused to delete the data. The Garante found that keeping the server and backup indefinitely, reading the messages and redirecting all mail breached lawfulness, data minimisation and storage limitation, and that the erasure requests were not properly answered. It ordered erasure of the individual mailbox data (save for retention needed for legal claims), ordered the redirection system to be brought into compliance within 60 days, and fined the company EUR 20,000.

A customer complained that Interflora Italia kept sending him promotional SMS messages after guest purchases on its e-commerce site, where giving a mobile number was mandatory and no consent for marketing was requested. His objection and access request to the company's DPO went unanswered, and the company also ignored the Garante's requests for information. The Garante found unlawful processing (no valid consent, breach of fairness, transparency and purpose limitation, failure to answer data subject rights requests). Because the company had remedied everything during the proceedings, it imposed no corrective measures but ordered a fine of EUR 40,000 and publication of the decision.

A municipal employee complained that the Comune di Roccaraso published on its website several council and administrative resolutions containing his name-related details and references to disputes arising from his employment. The Garante found that the municipality had no legal basis for this online dissemination, because it published the acts automatically in two website sections without checking whether a transparency obligation applied. The municipality also failed to give the complainant a proper written reply to his data-subject request. The Garante imposed a fine of EUR 2,000, ordered publication of the decision on its website, and restricted further dissemination of data that could identify the complainant.

The DPA rejected a police officer's complaint seeking the de-indexing of news articles concerning their criminal convictions. The DPA held that the articles were accurate, up to date, and of general interest due to the complainant's position as a public officer.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation in February 2025 at Automobilus International S.R.L., started after the company notified a personal data breach. A third party had illegally accessed the customer database by exploiting a vulnerability on one of the company's servers. The authority found the company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures and breached Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It fined the company 24,885 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to inform affected individuals about the incident and the remedial measures through a notice on its website's front page.
An accommodation provider was fined €1,200 for infringing Article 5(1)(c) GDPR by requiring guests, including children, to send photos of their IDs via WhatsApp.

The UODO President inspected Polskie Radio Szczecin after a 2022 news item identified a child victim of sexual abuse, who later took their own life.
